Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Mississippi statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we say so.

Mississippi property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Disagreement with a property valuation: request a hearing with the county Board of Supervisors (contact the county Chancery Clerk). (Property Tax FAQ - I disagree with the assessment; source)
  • Normally an appeal to the Board of Supervisors must be filed by the first Monday in August preceding the due date of the taxes. (Local Property Appraisal - Appeals; source)
  • Class I (single-family, owner-occupied residential real property) is assessed at 10% of true value; Class II (all other real property) at 15%. (Local Property Appraisal - five classes; source)
  • Assessment ratios are set by the Mississippi Constitution; tax = true value x assessment ratio x millage rate. (Property Tax FAQ - assessment ratio; source)
  • Tax Assessors must revalue real property at least once every four years; interior inspections of residences are not required. (Property Tax FAQ / Local Property Appraisal; source)
  • Unpaid real property taxes: property is subject to sale at the county tax auction; sales may be held first Monday in April or last Monday in August depending on county. (Property Tax FAQ / Local Property Appraisal; source)
  • Property taxes are due by February 1 following assessment; if unpaid, penalties and interest accrue. (Local Property Appraisal - Paying Property Taxes; source)

How to sell a Mississippi house when this applies to you

  1. Find out what the closing attorney needs. For an inherited or transferred house, that usually means the recorded deed or the probate paperwork that shows who owns it today.
  2. Get a payoff for any mortgage and the amount of any unpaid property tax. Both are paid from the sale proceeds at closing.
  3. Compare offers on what you net after repairs, commissions and closing costs, not on the headline price.
  4. If you want a fast, simple closing, ask for a written cash offer. We buy houses as-is, with no repairs and no agent commission. See we buy houses in Mississippi.

What a cash sale of a Mississippi house looks like, step by step

People often ask what actually happens after they contact a cash buyer. Here is the usual order of events for a house in Mississippi.

  1. Tell us about the property. Use the form on this page or call or text (424) 435-2326. We ask about the address, the condition and what is going on, such as a mortgage, back taxes, tenants or an estate.
  2. Get a written cash offer. We review the details and send a written offer. There is no obligation, and you can turn it down and owe us nothing.
  3. Pick your closing date. You choose the timeline. Some owners need weeks to move out, and others want to close quickly.
  4. The title company handles the paperwork. It checks ownership, pays off any mortgage and any unpaid property tax from the proceeds, and records the deed.
  5. You receive the proceeds. Our offers carry no agent commission, no fees and no closing costs to you.

Documents and information to have ready

You do not need everything below to get an offer, but each item makes the sale smoother and helps the title company work faster.

  • The deed or other proof of who owns the property today.
  • A recent mortgage statement or a payoff figure from the lender.
  • The latest property tax bill, plus any notice of unpaid or delinquent tax.
  • Homeowners association details, including dues and any unpaid assessments, if there is an association.
  • Current leases and the tenants' contact information, if the house is rented.
  • Estate paperwork, such as letters from the court, if you inherited the house.
  • A short list of known repairs. We buy as-is, but honest information avoids surprises.

Listing, selling it yourself or a cash offer: how they compare

Listing with an agent can bring a higher headline price when a house is in good shape and you have time. You pay the commission agreed in your listing contract, and you usually handle repairs, showings and the buyer's inspection requests. Closing depends on the buyer's financing.

Selling it yourself saves the listing commission but puts the marketing, the paperwork and the required Mississippi disclosures on you. You still need a title company or attorney to close.

Taking a cash offer trades some of the headline price for speed and certainty. We buy as-is, so there are no repairs, no showings and no financing contingency. It tends to fit owners dealing with foreclosure pressure, an inherited house, back taxes, tenants or a move on a deadline. Compare every option on what you net after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not on the headline price.

Questions to ask before you sell in Mississippi

  • Ask the title company what is owed and what the title company will need at closing.
  • Ask your lender for a written payoff figure good through your expected closing date, and ask whether there is a prepayment penalty.
  • Ask the county assessor whether a pending appeal or exemption affects the bill, and whether any exemption you receive ends when you sell.
  • If the house was inherited, ask the title company which court documents it needs before it will insure the sale.
  • If tenants live in the house, check the lease for its end date and any notice you must give.

These are general questions to start a conversation, not legal advice. Rules in Mississippi change, so confirm details with the official office or a Mississippi attorney or tax professional.

You choose the closing date within what the title company needs to clear ownership and payoffs.

No. We buy houses as-is, so you do not need to make repairs before selling.

Will you buy a house that has tenants in it?

Yes. We buy rentals as-is, occupied or vacant. Tell us about the lease when you request an offer.

What if I owe more on the mortgage than the house is worth?

Tell us the payoff figure. A sale that does not cover the loan may need lender approval, so ask your lender about a short sale before you sign anything.

It depends on who has legal authority to sign. The title company can tell you what court paperwork it needs.

Mississippi offers property tax relief for qualifying homeowners, and official sources explain the rules. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Applications are accepted only at the county Tax Assessor's office between January 1 and April 1. (Homestead Exemption | MS DOR; source)
  • Applicant must own and occupy the home as primary residence on January 1; ownership instrument must be filed with the Chancery Clerk before January 7. (Homestead Exemption | MS DOR; source)
  • Tier 1 regular exemption (under 65, not disabled): tax credit of up to $300 based on property value. (Homestead Exemption | MS DOR; source)
  • Tier 2 (age 65+ or totally disabled by Jan 1): exempt from taxes on the first $7,500 of assessed value; DOR FAQ states first $75,000 of true value. (Homestead Exemption | MS DOR; Property Tax FAQ; source)
  • Tier 3 total exemption covers service-connected totally disabled veterans, veterans 90+, and unremarried surviving spouses of those killed on active duty. (Homestead Exemption | MS DOR; source)
  • Once allowed, exemption carries over each year unless there is a change in ownership, use, occupancy or description (including deed changes, marriage, divorce, death) - reapplication may be required. (Homestead Exemption | MS DOR; source)
  • Exemption can be disallowed retroactively, e.g. for income tax noncompliance, or claiming homestead on more than one property. (Homestead Exemption | MS DOR; source)

Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Mississippi statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we say so.

Mississippi evictions follow notice and court steps set by state law. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Residential material noncompliance: landlord may give written notice terminating the rental agreement not less than 14 days after receipt if not remedied within 14 days; notice may be by email/text if agreed in writing. (Miss. Code 89-8-13(3) as in SB 2461 (2022); source)
  • Month-to-month tenancy may be terminated by written notice at least 30 days before termination; week-to-week by 7 days. (Miss. Code 89-8-19 as in SB 2461 (2022); source)
  • For nonpayment of rent, written notice requiring payment or possession after 3 days (89-7-27). (MS AG Consumer Guide (quotes 89-7-27); source)
  • Landlord files a sworn affidavit with the court; summons issues with a hearing not less than 3 nor more than 5 days from the summons date (89-7-31). (MS AG Consumer Guide (quotes 89-7-31); source)
  • Eviction hearing adjournments cannot extend the hearing beyond 45 days from filing. (MS AG Consumer Guide; source)
  • If judgment is for landlord the court issues a warrant to the sheriff/constable to put the landlord in possession; nonpayment warrant stayed if full rent, late fees and costs are paid within 10 days. (MS AG Consumer Guide (89-7-41, 89-7-45); source)
  • Tenant may appeal to circuit court within 30 days after possession is delivered by notice and bond. (MS AG Consumer Guide; source)
  • Residential landlord-tenant rights, notice and eviction rules (89-8, 89-7) apply to occupants; holdover tenants can be removed through the justice-court process described under eviction-process. (MS AG Consumer Guide: Residential Landlord and Tenant Act; source)
  • Month-to-month tenancy needs 30 days' written notice to terminate. (Miss. Code 89-8-19 as in SB 2461 (2022); source)

  1. Tell us about the property. Use the form on this page or call or text (424) 435-2326. We ask about the address, the condition and what is going on, such as a mortgage, back taxes, tenants or an estate.
  2. Get a written cash offer. We review the details and send a written offer. There is no obligation, and you can turn it down and owe us nothing.
  3. Pick your closing date. You choose the timeline. Some owners need weeks to move out, and others want to close quickly.
  4. The title company handles the paperwork. It checks ownership, pays off any mortgage and any unpaid property tax from the proceeds, and records the deed.
  5. You receive the proceeds. Our offers carry no agent commission, no fees and no closing costs to you.

  • The latest property tax bill, plus any notice of unpaid or delinquent tax.

  • Current leases and the tenants' contact information, if the house is rented.
  • Estate paperwork, such as letters from the court, if you inherited the house.

Listing with an agent can bring a higher headline price when a house is in good shape and you have time. You pay the commission agreed in your listing contract, and you usually handle repairs, showings and the buyer's inspection requests. Closing depends on the buyer's financing.

Selling it yourself saves the listing commission but puts the marketing, the paperwork and the required Mississippi disclosures on you. You still need a title company or attorney to close.

Yes. We buy rentals as-is, occupied or vacant. Tell us about the lease when you request an offer.

What if I owe more on the mortgage than the house is worth?

Tell us the payoff figure. A sale that does not cover the loan may need lender approval, so ask your lender about a short sale before you sign anything.

Can I sell an inherited house before probate is finished?

It depends on who has legal authority to sign. The title company can tell you what court paperwork it needs.

Is there any cost to request an offer?

No. Requesting an offer is free and carries no obligation.
